title: Tail Latency Investigation and Mitigation Playbook
author: Nina Patel
content:
Overview:

This playbook describes a reproducible, prioritized workflow for investigating, mitigating, and preventing tail-latency regressions in the Redwood serving runtime. It covers measurement methodology, diagnostic commands, quick mitigations, kernel-scheduler knobs, benchmark repro recipes, canary/rollout guidance, alerting rules, and a checklist for post-incident follow-up.

Why tail latency matters:

- SLO impact: p99 and p99.9 directly affect user-facing latency for streaming and non-streaming workloads; a small number of high-latency requests can cause downstream timeouts and user-visible errors.
- Cost and capacity: excessive tail latency reduces effective throughput and increases idle GPU time (KV cache churn, smaller batch efficiency).
- Regression vectors: model changes (longer context), quantization shifts, kernel changes, misconfigured batchers, network spikes, and KV cache thrash.

SLOs and thresholds (company-standard baseline):

- p50 <= 35ms (token generation path, hosted small models)
- p95 <= 120ms
- p99 <= 450ms
- p99.9 <= 1200ms
- Return-to-service target for critical customer routes: p99 < 500ms within 30 minutes of detection unless escalated.

Measurement and instrumentation guidelines:

- Use downstream, request-scoped tracing (trace events: request_enqueue, batch_start, kernel_launch, kvcache_lookup, kvcache_miss, dll_fetch, response_stream_start).
- Emit microsecond-resolution histograms for request_duration_seconds and per-substage timers (enqueue, batch_wait, kernel_exec, kvcache_latency).
- Label dimensions: model_name, model_variant (quant/float), deployment_zone, backend_node_id, route, request_size_tokens, client_tier.
- Define rolling windows: 1m / 5m / 1h for alerts/analysis.

Key Prometheus / Thanos queries (examples):

- p99 latency (5m):
  histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model_name))

- Tail contribution by substage (5m):
  sum(rate(kernel_exec_seconds_sum[5m])) by (model_name) / sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_sum[5m])) by (model_name)

- Hot-node identification (p99 per backend):
  topk(10, histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, backend_node_id)))

Diagnostic workflow (ordered):

1) Confirm alert and scope: identify affected routes, model variants, and time range.
2) Pull dashboards: p50/p95/p99 heatmap over zones and backend_node_id.
3) Correlate upstream events: deployments, kernel rollouts, autoscaler events, config changes.
4) Triangulate using traces: filter traces for requests with duration > p99 threshold, inspect span timeline for long gaps.
5) Reproduce with targeted load: run the micro-workload for the failing route at 2x p99 arrival rate to reproduce.
6) Mitigate (see quick mitigations).
7) Root-cause analysis and permanent fix.

Quick mitigations (emergency steps to restore SLOs):

- Route-level rollback: pin the route to previous model_variant (fastest rollback if regression due to model or quantization).
- Backpressure tuning: reduce max_concurrency for the route to reduce batching head-of-line blocking (example: max_concurrency 32 -> 16).
- Autoscaler pulse: scale up dedicated pool by +20% capacity for 10–30 minutes to absorb tail churn.
- Batcher drain and restart: rotate batcher workers on affected nodes one-at-a-time to clear strays.
- Fallback policy: switch to a lower-context / smaller model variant with preserved semantic behavior.

Emergency CLI snippets:

- Rollback a route to pinned variant:
  redwood routes update --route-id r-1234 --model-variant stable-v1

- Temporarily reduce concurrency on route (examples):
  redwood routes update --route-id r-1234 --max-concurrency 16

- Force autoscale increase (dedicated pools):
  redwood pools scale --pool-id p-12 --desired-instances 12 --reason "tail-latency mitigation"

Kernel / scheduler tuning matrix (guidance):

- If p99 kernel_exec is dominating and kernel shapes are small (short seq): favor smaller-launch latency-optimized kernels: kernel.flags = ["low-launch-latency"] and kernel.batch_size_hint = 8.
- If batch wait contributes > 20% to p99: increase max_batch_size and reduce batch_timeout_ms to prioritize throughput: max_batch_size += 50%, batch_timeout_ms -= 10ms (observe cost).
- If KV cache miss ratio > 2% and kvcache_latency contributes to tail: enable per-node hot-key prefetch and reduce kvcache_eviction_pressure: kvcache.eviction_target = 0.6 -> 0.75.

Example scheduler tune table (text-representation):

- Scenario: Single-node hot tail due to kernel spikes\  Action: reduce kernel-concurrency on node, set kernel.flags to low-launch-latency\  Expected effect: reduced p99 kernel latency, lower throughput efficiency
- Scenario: Global increase in batch_wait\  Action: increase batch_timeout_ms by 5–15ms, raise max_batch_size for non-latency routes\  Expected effect: shifts work to larger batches, improves token cost and average latency

Profiling playbook (what to collect):

- Collect a minimal trace set for 50 failing requests (p99 class) and 50 matching successful requests. Use distributed tracing export and local perf tools (nsys for NVIDIA).
- For GPU traces: nsys capture focused on kernel launch and memcpy with --trace=cuda,nvtx and symbols for runtime.
- For CPU/batcher: perf record --call-graph dwarf -p <pid> for 60s on affected batcher process.

Profiling commands (examples):

- Trace collection (request scoped):
  redwood debug collect-trace --request-id <req-id> --out /tmp/trace-<req-id>.json

- GPU capture (container):
  docker exec -it runtime-worker bash -c "nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=none -- ./bin/runtime-worker --trace-target <backend_node_id>"

- Aggregated flamegraphs (CPU):
  perf script | FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
  FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg

Benchmarking repro harness (step-by-step):

1) Isolate route in an internal staging deployment with the same model_variant and quantization flags.
2) Seed KV cache with representative prefixes using seed-client:
   seed-client --model my-model --prefix-file samples/prefixes.txt --parallelism 8 --rate 50/s
3) Replay a recorded production arrival trace (5m) at 1x/2x p99 rate using replay-tool:
   replay-tool --trace artifacts/prod-2026-01-11.trace --replay-rate 2.0 --concurrency 4 --route r-1234
4) Monitor metrics (Prometheus + runtime traces) and capture traces on failing runs.

Canary and rollout mitigation plan (safeguards):

- Canary settings for kernel/scheduler changes:
  - Canary size: 2% of traffic or <= 2 instances in each zone.
  - Canary observation period: 30 minutes with p99 and error rate gating.
  - Roll forward criteria: no p99 regression > 15% and error rate increase < 0.05% over baseline.
  - Rollback criteria: p99 > 25% above baseline or error rate delta >= 0.1%.

- A/B and gradual ramp guidance: use step ramps of 5–10% every 15 minutes with automated rollback hooks.

Alerting rules (examples):

- Critical: p99(past 5m) > SLO by 30% for two consecutive evaluation windows (5m) -> page SRE and runtime-oncall.
- Warning: p99 increase > 15% -> slack channel #runtime-performance for triage.

Example alert rule (pseudo-Prometheus):
  ALERT TailLatencyCritical
  IF histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route)) > (slo_route_p99 * 1.3)
  FOR 10m
  LABELS {severity="page"}
  ANNOTATIONS {runbook="/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/tail-latency-investigation-and-mitigation-playbook-2026"}

Post-incident checklist and RCA steps:

- Save raw traces and profiling captures to the incident artifact bucket with tags (incident_id, route, timeframe).
- Record all mitigation steps in the incident timeline (who did what and why).
- Run the reproducible benchmark recipe and attach artifacts to RCA.
- Identify preventative engineering work: kernel patch, batcher improvement, KV cache policy, rollout gating changes.
- Schedule an engineering task with owner and target ETA; include automated regression test in the perf-suite pipeline.

Ownership, escalation, and runbook contacts:

- First responder: runtime-oncall (rotating SRE)
- Secondary: serving-runtime team (pager: @serving-runtime)
- Tertiary: profiling-and-evals team for deep kernel work

Dashboards and recommended panels:

- Route performance overview: p50/p95/p99 horizon chart by route and model_variant.
- Node hotlist: table of p99 by backend_node_id, memory pressure, gpu_utilization, kvcache_eviction_rate.
- Substage waterfall: stacked bar showing percent time spent in enqueue/batch_wait/kernel_exec/kvcache.

Appendix A — Example JSON trace filter (for trace-collector):

{
  "filter": {
    "min_duration_ms": 450,
    "labels": {"route": "r-1234", "model_variant": "candidate-v2"}
  },
  "limit": 200
}

Appendix B — Frequently observed root causes and remedies:

- Kernel launch variance due to JIT/kernel selection: roll back recent kernel mapper changes or pin kernel profile for the model.
- KV cache churn after model size increase: enlarge node-local cache or change eviction policy.
- Batcher stall caused by skewed client arrival patterns: enable adaptive batching per-client and cap single-client concurrency.
